title: Disclosure, Boundaries, and Listener Reactions
learningGoals: Separate observed reaction from a guess

deeperExplanation.question: What if someone reacts badly to my boundary?
deeperExplanation.answer: A boundary gives information about what you need; it does not control another person. You can repeat the request, change the setting, seek support or decide to leave the exchange. Consider the relationship and practical consequences. You do not have to explain your entire history to justify a simple speaking preference. Their reaction can help you choose how much access or trust to offer next.

sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Disclosure, Boundaries, and Listener Reactions. Someone finishes your sentence or offers advice you did not ask for. You want to explain what helps, but worry that doing so will make the moment uncomfortable.

In this session, we will choose how much to disclose, state a clear preference, and separate observed reaction from a guess. I will explain the idea, show a visual example, and invite you to try it in a small experience of your own. You can ask me a question or switch to reading at any point. We will finish by choosing what, if anything, you want to take into a real conversation.

sections.narration: You can decide how much to share about your speech. Disclosure is an option, not a requirement for participation. A boundary can focus on the immediate need: please let me finish, or I may take a little longer and I want to say this in my own words. You can be warm and direct at the same time.

sections.narration:
Someone finishes your sentence or offers advice you did not ask for. You want to explain what helps, but worry that doing so will make the moment uncomfortable.

Listener reactions are varied and sometimes unclear. A glance, pause or expression does not tell you everything they think. You can check an interpretation, state a need or choose not to engage further. If someone is repeatedly unkind, you do not have to turn their response into a lesson about your own confidence.

sections.narration: Unspoken hope: They should know not to finish for me. Stated preference: I appreciate you trying to help. I would like to finish the sentence myself. You can acknowledge intent while being clear about impact. Now consider a short check. What is true about disclosure? Choose an option when you are ready; I will explain the distinction.

exercise.label: Guided rehearsal
exercise.scenario: Someone finishes your sentence or offers advice you did not ask for. You want to explain what helps, but worry that doing so will make the moment uncomfortable.
partnerPrompts: I finish your sentence, trying to help. What would you like me to do?
I look uncertain. How could you check what I understood?
I interrupt again. State a boundary or choose how to leave the exchange.

sections.narration: You do not have to disclose in order to earn patience, and a boundary does not guarantee the other person will respond well. Their reaction gives information about the relationship, not a verdict about you. A changed, unchanged or uncertain experience is information, not a grade. You do not have to report relief for this attempt to count as exploration.

sections.narration: Use one preference statement when it serves you. Record what you asked, what was actually said and what you choose next. During focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one tool. In an everyday conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; you do not have to monitor the tool throughout the exchange.
